population.note: FICTIONAL. Totals, from ~274M adults: 32.5% current ≈ 89.1M; 43.5% ever ≈ 119.2M; used and now off 11.0% ≈ 30.1M; never used ≈ 154.8M. Ever-use rose 8.0 pts, inside the 10.5 limit, and current rose 7.5. Cycling: ≈15.5 pts of current users are on a second or later course, and ≈4.5 pts of the off-now group restarted at least once and then stopped again. (15.5+4.5)/43.5 ≈ 46% cycled. That fits the parent's ~35% one-year persistence and 36–47% restart rate. Monthly MariTide raised persistence among its users, and the 2034 employer retreat pushed it the other way. Who is off now (≈30.1M): ≈8.5M lost employer obesity coverage in the 2034 plan year and did not move to cash or imports; ≈4.5M are on a medical pause (bone pause, DEXA findings, gallbladder); ≈6M stopped over GI effects or 'the grey'; the rest finished a course, are pregnant, or lapsed. Age check, bands 52M/92M/61M/69M: 18–29 21% = 10.9M; 30–49 37.5% = 34.5M; 50–64 47.8% = 29.2M; 65+ 21% = 14.5M; total ≈ 89.1M. Under-30 use rose 13.5→21%. The drivers were cheap imported pens sold through group chats, off-label and then on-label vaping cessation, and 'quiet' subscriptions. The 65+ rise follows each new age cohort aging into the Part D benefit. Income: the bottom third went from 21 to 29.5%, mostly through imported generics at $5–30, and Medicaid enrolment in the 31 adopting states plus DC grew without any new state joining. The middle third lost the most employer coverage and moved to cash. Never-users (~155M) are now concentrated among rural residents of non-expansion states, people with contraindications, refusers by conviction, and adults under 30 who neither vape nor diet. Pediatric: 1.1% of ~73M ≈ 800k on-label adolescents. Teen use of imported pens for vaping cessation is unmeasured; poison-centre data suggest tens of thousands. About two children in five now live with a parent who is on the drug or cycling.

access.public_coverage: FICTIONAL. The Part D obesity benefit and the Medicaid 90% match have the same structure as in 2032. No new state adopted the continuation standard: it is still 31 states plus DC. Under the HHS–manufacturer agreement of Oct 2033, the Medicare and Medicaid rate for semaglutide and tirzepatide fell from $199 to $169 from Jan 2034. Retatrutide and MariTide sit on a $249 Part D tier. The $50 beneficiary copay is unchanged. Medicare pays 17.5% of fills ≈ 15.6M users (14.3M aged 65+ and 1.3M disabled under 65): ≈6.6M diabetes or cardiac, ≈9.0M obesity. The blended Medicare rate is 0.89×$169 + 0.11×$249 ≈ $178. Obesity benefit gross: 9.0M × $178 × 12 ≈ $19.2B. Beneficiaries pay 9.0M × $50 × 12 ≈ $5.4B, so the program pays ≈$13.8B a year. That is almost exactly the CBO's $14B annual average, because higher volume offset the lower price. All Medicare incretin fills: 15.6M × $178 × 12 ≈ $33.3B gross. Medicaid pays 12.8% of fills ≈ 11.4M users × ≈$172 blended × 12 ≈ $23.5B gross before supplemental rebates. Medicare is still the largest single buyer.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 120+ semaglutide brands at $5–30/month, generic oral semaglutide at $8–25, and early tirzepatide copies for export. China: generic semaglutide and tirzepatide, and the API for most of the world's gray trade. Canada: generic semaglutide at CAD 45–75/month. Mexico: border pharmacies in Tijuana, Nogales and Ciudad Juárez sell branded-generic semaglutide at $40–70. Brazil, Turkey and Egypt also have generics. In the US, FDA issued complete response letters to the first semaglutide ANDAs in Mar 2033 over peptide-related impurity and immunogenicity data. The 2031 settlements were keyed to final approval, so US entry slipped to an unknown date, and resubmissions are under review.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Prices are declining under management. Under the Oct 2033 agreement, portal injectable semaglutide and tirzepatide fell from $199–279 to $179–249. The oral starter dose (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) stays at $149, and higher oral doses cost $169–199. Retatrutide is $349 direct ($1,499 list) and MariTide $299/month direct. List prices hold: Wegovy is still $1,349. PBM net is ≈$155–170. Payer mix of ≈89.1M users: commercial 27.5% (24.5M, of whom ≈17.0M are under diabetes, ASCVD, OSA, CKD or MASH codes and ≈7.5M under remaining obesity coverage); Medicare 17.5% (15.6M); Medicaid 12.8% (11.4M); cash/direct 28.2% (25.1M, including ≈4.2M 'quiet/focus' subscribers and ≈1.6M nicotine-cessation users); imported/counterfeit 14.0% (12.5M). Sum 89.1M = 100%. Imports more than tripled from 3.8M once the 2033 generic failed to arrive and employers withdrew coverage. Seizure testing suggests about one imported pen in six is substandard or falsified. Of employers still covering weight management, ≈80% use gating. Employers that dropped coverage kept the diabetes and cardiac codes, so home sleep tests and repeat A1c draws for 'code eligibility' have surged. The 503B exclusion and 503A injunction stand.

drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. next_gen_launch (monthly_or_implant) is met by MariTide. It was under review at the start, and FDA approved it in Jun 2033 on 72-week DEXA data, with ≈20% mean loss at 72 weeks, monthly dosing and body-composition monitoring in the label. Amgen supply reached ≈3.8M US users by end-2034. No implant is filed or approved. Survodutide was approved in Feb 2033 at its PDUFA date with a DEXA requirement. Of the new_indications, nicotine is a full approval: the SHAPS-endpoint cessation trial read out in Apr 2033, the sNDA for oral semaglutide was filed in Jul 2033, and approval came in Oct 2034, 15 months later after an extended review of neuropsychiatric data. In the trial, 6.8% of the active arm crossed the SHAPS threshold at 24 weeks against 4.9% on placebo, which was not significant. mood_and_motivation is honoured by a filing, as the rules allow. Lilly filed low-dose Foundayo for binge-eating disorder with a craving-related-distress secondary endpoint in Apr 2034, and the PDUFA date falls in 2035. Telehealth brands sell 'quiet mind' under wellness wording and, since Oct 2034, quote the cessation label's craving claim. Bimagrumab combinations are still in phase 3, with a filing expected in 2035. Best efficacy is unchanged at 30%. US incretin revenue ≈ $158B (≈76.6M paying users × ≈$172 average net × 12); ex-US ≈ $24B and eroding; total ≈ $182B.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common effect and the leading reason people stop. With monthly MariTide, nausea cannot be cut short by skipping a dose, and early-titration vomiting accounts for most of its discontinuations.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; MariTide label requires slow titration and warns of prolonged GI effects; gastroparesis caution retained.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Rising in absolute terms with the larger 65+ and high-dose population.
No causal confirmation, and absolute risk is low. Reporting is more confounded than ever because imported product is often unidentified.

With ≈14.3M Medicare users aged 65+, claims models estimate ≈1.6M long-term older users meet sarcopenia criteria. Lean mass is ~30–40% of weight lost in untrained users over 50. MariTide DEXA data fall in the middle of that range.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class label retained. The 12 mg retatrutide, amycretin, survodutide and MariTide labels require body-composition monitoring. CMS still requires annual DEXA for long-term 65+ users, and MA strength benefits keep expanding.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ≈7.2M users aged 65+ have more than 2 years' use. At ~0.6%/yr baseline × 0.35 excess, that is ≈15,000 excess hip fractures a year against ~300,000 total, plus the vertebral tail in cycling postmenopausal women aged 50–64, which grew as employer drop-offs added cycles. Mobile capacity has cut DEXA waits to 8–16 weeks in the Sun Belt.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Unchanged: bone endpoints are required in all filings, and the CMS 90-day bone-pause code continues. Gated private plans are not bound by it. DOJ civil case against Novo unresolved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label; FDA warnings mention; no class determination.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association, including in the cessation trial population.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia, 'the grey')
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal. The observational top-dose figure still stands at ~12% versus ~5%. The randomised low-dose cessation trial found 6.8% versus 4.9%, a difference that was not significant. Low dose therefore looks mild and top dose looks worse, and the dose-dependence reading holds. The ≈4.2M 'quiet' subscribers are still unmeasured independently.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The cessation label carries SHAPS monitoring language. FTC 2031 consent orders still bar 'anxiety treatment' claims. No class label change.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The 2034 employer retreat produced the largest single wave of stops (≈8.5M not replaced) and with it millions of regain episodes.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The CMS bone-pause code covers Medicare only. The Seventh Circuit has not ruled on the Indiana waiver.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Common in high-loss older users and in import users with no clinician contact.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Professional guidance and the Part D counselling screen; no FDA action.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~8 years; adolescent exposure; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About twelve years of follow-up. Sponsors submitted the full adolescent bone-accrual data in Nov 2034, and FDA review is pending. Cycling still looks worse for bone than continuous use.

Now a public-health story. Poison-centre calls about imported incretins roughly tripled from 2032 to 2034. The May 2034 cluster of insulin-contaminated counterfeit pens caused ≈1,100 ED visits for severe hypoglycaemia across six states and 14 deaths. Dosing errors from concentrated multi-dose vials and pen-cartridge refills are common, and so are injection-site infections. One seized pen in six is substandard or falsified.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: CDC Health Alert Network advisory (May 2034), expanded import alerts and parcel seizures. The 'Safe Pens' authentication bill passed the House but stalled in the Senate. Individuals are still not prosecuted.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A few percent, higher at 12 mg; usually transient.

safety_ledger.effect: Falls and frailty-related injury in older users
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Fall-related ED visits remain elevated in 65+ users with more than 2 years' use, and the absolute number has risen with the population.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Fall-risk screening is mandatory in the Part D counselling visit.

safety_ledger.effect: Adverse body-composition cycling (fat-dominant regain after lean-dominant loss)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Larger exposure because the employer retreat forced cycles on people over 50. DEXA cohorts still show less lean mass and more visceral fat at the same weight.

safety_ledger.effect: Heart-rate elevation at high triple-agonist doses
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A mean rise of several bpm at 12 mg retatrutide, with arrhythmia significance unclear. Survodutide shows a similar small rise.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Precautionary labelling; cardiovascular outcomes trials ongoing.

food_and_beverage.state: With one adult in three on the drug, salty-snack volume falls ~4%/yr and confectionery ~5%. The convenience-store channel is hit hardest because its baskets were built on snacks, sugary drinks, beer and nicotine, which are all falling together. Several regional c-store chains have refitted space for protein, fortified dairy and cold cases. Candy portfolios bought by private equity in 2031–32 are being consolidated, and their brands now aim at the ≈30M off-drug and the never-users.

alcohol.state: Sixth straight year of spirits volume decline, and beer is also down. Nicotine is the bigger shock: e-cigarette volume fell an estimated ~15% in 2034 as off-label and then on-label cessation spread, and vape-shop closures are visible in college towns and strip malls. Cigarette volume is declining faster than trend. Non-alcoholic drinks keep growing.

restaurants.state: Traffic is roughly flat to slightly down. Half portions and gram-priced bowls are standard. Weekend 'full table' nights work because monthly-shot users in their fourth-week trough, and people on a dose holiday, come out for them. Value buffets keep closing, and heritage rooms in Atlanta, Memphis and Houston hold.

apparel.state: The employer retreat triggered a new wave of size churn: middle-income regainers in 2034. Rental and resale built for cycling keeps growing, and mid-market brands hedge with stretch fits.

fitness.state: Growing. DEXA-plus-coaching chains and mobile vans have added capacity, which is why waits are shorter. Prescribed lifting is an MA line item. Staff qualified for older lifters remain the constraint.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage fell from 66% to 47% for the 2034 plan year. The reasons: the generic slip, a +7% pharmacy trend, fall and fracture claims, and the knowledge that Medicare picks people up at 65. Plans kept the diabetes, ASCVD, OSA, CKD and MASH codes, so eligibility now runs through diagnosis, and home sleep tests and prediabetes re-testing have surged. Wellness surcharges continue. Carriers are asking whether ACA preventive-coverage rules will force no-cost coverage of the new cessation indication.

pharma.state: Volume is up ~30% while net price fell ~10%, so US revenue grew to ≈$158B. Lilly leads, and Amgen's MariTide is the fastest-growing launch and the favourite of gated employers because adherence is automatic. Novo holds Medicare share and the cessation label. Indian and Chinese generic makers profit through gray channels and await the ANDA resubmissions.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Normalised further. Among insured adults over 40, being on is unremarkable. A monthly shot leaves no pen in the fridge, so being on has become invisible. Being off needs a reason, and the most common reason in 2034 is 'my job dropped it'. Visible regain among middle-income workers is read as a lost plan, and the forward stoop in over-60s as a scan that came too late.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Use is converging by income (29.5 vs 35%), but tiers are hardening by payer. The coded and Medicare users get monitored regimens. Cash users get the $149 oral starter or portal injectables. The bottom third increasingly buys Indian generics through group chats, without a scan or a pharmacist. In El Paso and San Diego, trips across the border for pens have become routine, the way trips for insulin once were.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Protein-first shared meals are the default, and hosts plan for 'on' guests. Monthly-shot households schedule celebrations for week four, when drug levels are at their lowest. Church potlucks and Sunday full-table dinners continue as heritage.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: The on/off/pausing field on apps now has a 'steerable' option, meaning a daily oral that can be skipped, which people read as having some control over their own appetite and mood. 'Unmedicated' is still a niche filter.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Medicalised and assumed to be managed. The backlash coalition is the same size in absolute terms. Its campaigns now centre on the counterfeit deaths, which it uses as evidence that the system pushed poor people to the mail, and on weigh-in welfare.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. Roughly 8–9M Americans are on top-dose triple, dual or MariTide regimens. At the observational ~7-point excess that implies ~550–650k excess cases of clinically meaningful anhedonia if the association is causal. The low-dose RCT figure (6.8 vs 4.9%, not significant) is the one telehealth brands cite. Surveys find about one user in three has taken a deliberate 'dose holiday' in the past year, and about half of 'quiet' subscribers say they titrate by feel.
interior_life.framing: A complaint people manage. 'The grey' is talk-show material, clinicians say 'reward modulation', and people talk about doses the way they talk about caffeine: 'I'm down to half for the wedding.' Retail still sells 'quiet mind', now quoting the cessation label's craving claim. The monthly shot has turned 'steerability' into a selling point: daily orals are marketed as the form you can adjust.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Gated employers and fleets that still cover weight management prefer MariTide because it reports 100% adherence automatically. Sales, hospitality and creative workers move back to daily orals so they can dose down before pitches and service peaks. 'Focus' subscriptions stay in HR catalogues. Some unions negotiate the right to switch formulation without restarting the gating clock.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Late-night comedy and a network sitcom ('Week Four') make the grey ordinary. Festivals and destination weddings advertise 'holiday-friendly' dates. Critics' 'grey era' label has become a cliché. Demand for intense stimulus, such as spicy food, loud rooms and extreme sports, keeps growing.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Couples plan around the trough: monthly users report week four as the week they feel desire, and sex therapists chart injection dates. Pharmacies still stock 'restart' anti-nausea packs for people coming back from oral holidays. Being 'on Quiet' while a partner is off is a standard topic in counselling.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The fight is now between people whose plan covers them through a diagnosis code and people whose plan covers nothing. Democrats push importation legalisation and generic acceleration. Republicans push parcel interdiction and Safe Pens. Neither passes. After the May cluster, senators held hearings with the families of people who died. Senior groups have moved on from DEXA capacity to fracture costs.

state.regulatory_posture: FDA is data-demanding but approving: MariTide and survodutide with DEXA requirements, and the cessation indication with SHAPS language. It issued ANDA complete response letters over peptide impurities. Import enforcement is louder but still selective: CDC advisories, parcel seizures, no individual prosecutions and no importation law. FTC still acts through consent orders.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Unchanged structure. The Part D obesity benefit, now at $169 for semaglutide and tirzepatide and $249 for the top tier, keeps its $50 copay. The 90% Medicaid match continues in 31 states plus DC. No new state action. No mandate.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: The CMS continuation standard is unchanged: 80% PDC, verified six-monthly weights, the 5% response threshold, annual DEXA for long-term 65+ users and the 90-day bone pause. MariTide users meet the PDC requirement automatically. The Indiana and Arkansas 12-month rules continue. Private gating covers ~80% of remaining employer obesity coverage. BMI-linked wellness surcharges continue.
state.workforce_or_military: DOT sleep-apnea screening still steers drivers toward tirzepatide, and the OSA code is now also how many workers keep coverage. Fleets favour MariTide. The Army is still contested; the Air Force grants waivers after 12 months' stability.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Chinese API and Indian finished product supply most of the US gray market. US–India 'parcel cooperation' produced joint seizure statistics but no legal channel. Section 232 tariffs remain. Lilly's 12 mg allocation eased in 2033 after new North Carolina fill-finish capacity came online.

events.event: FDA issues complete response letters to the first generic semaglutide applications, citing peptide impurity and immunogenicity data; because the 2031 settlements were keyed to final approval, the expected 2033 US generic slips with no new date

FDA approves Amgen's MariTide, the first once-a-month obesity injection, with about 20% average loss and mandatory body-composition scans; gated employer plans begin preferring it because adherence reporting becomes automatic

HHS and manufacturers agree a step-down: Medicare and Medicaid pay $169 a month for semaglutide and tirzepatide from January, portal injectables fall to $179–249, and the $149 oral starter and list prices are unchanged

Benefits surveys show employer weight-loss coverage falling from 66% to 47% for the 2034 plan year as large employers keep only diabetes, heart, sleep-apnea and kidney codes; an estimated 8.5 million people lose coverage and do not replace it

CDC health alert after counterfeit semaglutide pens containing insulin send about 1,100 people to emergency rooms with severe low blood sugar across six states and kill 14; seizures show one imported pen in six is falsified or substandard

FDA approves oral semaglutide as an aid to quitting smoking and vaping, with a craving-reduction claim and mood-monitoring language; Lilly's filing of low-dose Foundayo for binge-eating disorder is already under review, and a national survey finds one user in three took a 'dose holiday' this year

open_tensions: Two tiers have hardened. Employer coverage now runs through diabetes, cardiac, sleep-apnea and kidney codes, which rewards diagnosis-shopping. Meanwhile ≈12.5M Americans, disproportionately middle- and bottom-income, inject imports with no scan, no pharmacist and a one-in-six chance of a bad pen. Congress has neither legalised import nor sealed the mail.

The generic semaglutide resubmissions are pending with no date. Every budget, from Part D to state Medicaid to employer plans, is still priced as if entry were imminent. If entry slips again, the managed-decline deal is the only lever left. If it happens, the whole public bill reprices at once.

The new cessation label may trigger ACA preventive-coverage rules, which would require no-cost coverage of the same molecule that employers just dropped for obesity. A tobacco-cessation route into coverage, with its own SHAPS questions, is the next fight.

Monthly MariTide makes adherence automatic just as dose holidays have become a mainstream way of managing 'the grey'. Gated plans prefer the form that users cannot steer, and the 15,000-a-year hip-fracture excess and its Part A costs remain outside any budget score.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide is on the US market; generic_us remains false.
Wegovy's list price remains $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.
Oral starting doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) are still $149 a month cash through the federal direct-pricing portal (launched as TrumpRx) and manufacturer direct channels.

The CMS continuation standard is still in force with its 80% PDC, six-monthly verified weigh-ins, 5% threshold, annual DEXA for long-term 65+ users and the 90-day bone-pause code, adopted by the same 31 states plus DC.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.

prose.headline: One in Three, and the Generic Never Came: Inside America's Two-Tier Shot, From the Monthly Pen to the Mailbox
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2034 one American adult in three is on an incretin drug. More of them than ever cannot tell you who made it. The generic semaglutide everyone had planned around for 2033 did not arrive. In March of that year the FDA sent the first applicants back over impurity and immunogenicity data. The 2031 patent settlements were tied to final approval, so the date simply disappeared. Every budget built on that date, from Part D to state Medicaid to the large employers, had to be redone without it.

The employers redid theirs first. For the 2034 plan year, weight-management coverage fell from two-thirds of employers to under half. Most kept paying for the same molecules under diabetes, heart, sleep-apnea, kidney and liver codes and stopped paying for them under obesity. The result is a coverage system that runs on diagnoses. Home sleep tests and repeat A1c draws have become a way to keep a prescription. About eight and a half million people lost their plan coverage and did not replace it. Millions more went to the federal portal, where a January price step-down put the injectables at $179 to $249 while the oral starter stayed at $149. More than twelve million went to the mail.

The mail is now a public-health story. Indian brands sell at five to thirty dollars, Chinese API underlies most of them, and Juárez and Tijuana pharmacies sell branded generics to day-trippers. In May a batch of counterfeit pens filled with insulin sent about eleven hundred people to emergency rooms in six states, and fourteen died. Seizure testing found roughly one imported pen in six was falsified or substandard. The House passed a pen-authentication bill and the Senate let it stall. Nobody has been prosecuted for injecting. Democrats talk about legalising imports, Republicans about sealing the parcels, and neither has the votes.

The public programmes look almost unchanged from outside. Medicare still charges seniors a $50 copay, but it now pays $169 for the older molecules instead of $199. Higher volume has absorbed the saving, so the obesity benefit costs about what the CBO said it would. The continuation standard still weighs people at pharmacy kiosks and still requires annual bone scans for long-term seniors. Mobile scanners have cut the waits, though not to zero. The excess hip-fracture count has risen with the population, to about fifteen thousand a year. It is billed to Part A, and nobody's score includes it.

The newest drug is monthly. Amgen's MariTide was approved in June 2033 and produces about a fifth of body weight lost with one injection every four weeks. Gated employers like it because it reports perfect adherence to them. Users are more ambivalent, because a monthly shot cannot be skipped. That matters now that 'the grey' has become ordinary conversation. A third of users say they took a deliberate dose holiday this year, for a wedding, a tour, a pitch or a honeymoon. Daily pills are now marketed as the form you can steer. Monthly-shot couples have learned that week four, when the drug level is lowest, is when they want each other. A network sitcom is named after it.

In October the FDA approved oral semaglutide to help people quit smoking and vaping, with a craving claim and a mood-monitoring paragraph. Vape shops in college towns are closing. The 'quiet mind' subscriptions, now four million strong, quote the new label within days. A binge-eating filing for low-dose Foundayo is under review, and it is the closest anyone has come to selling calm under a medical indication.

Being on the drug is unremarkable. Being off it is explained by naming an employer.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Denise Ortega's dental office dropped the obesity code in January. Her A1c is 5.6. That is not high enough, and she has stopped trying to make it higher.

At 6:40 she drives her mother to the mobile DEXA van parked behind St. Pius. Her mother has a Medicare card, a $50 copay and a folder with every scan since 2031. While they wait, the woman beside them complains that the April kiosk weigh-in at Walgreens logged her in her boots.

At noon Denise eats half a burrito standing up. By two she is hungry the way she was before 2032. She had forgotten that kind of hunger.

After work she crosses the Bridge of the Americas. The farmacia on Avenida Juárez has the boxes behind glass, $52 for a month. The pharmacist turns one over and shows her the hologram and the lot number, then checks it against a list taped to the register. Since May everyone checks the list. She buys two months.

The line back into El Paso takes an hour. The customs officer sees the boxes, says 'personal use?', and waves her on.

At home her son Mateo, sixteen, is at the kitchen table with a friend whose cousin sells pens for vaping. Denise says nothing yet. She puts the boxes in the butter drawer next to the ones from March.

She dials the first dose and holds the pen against her stomach. She counts to ten the way the video says, and then waits a moment longer before getting up.
